title: Ezekiel 46:19–24
context: The guide brings Ezekiel to the priests’ rooms on the north side and shows him a place at the west end where the priests boil the trespass and sin offerings and bake the meal offering, so that these holy portions are not carried into the outer court (46:19–20; compare 44:19, 29). He then shows four enclosed corner courts in the outer court, forty by thirty cubits, with hearths along their walls: the “boiling houses” where the ministers of the house cook the sacrifices of the people (46:21–24). A cubit is about 18 inches, or 46 centimeters.

verses.text: Then he brought me through the entry, which was at the side of the gate, into the holy rooms for the priests, which looked toward the north. Behold, there was a place on the back part westward.
verses.arminianNotes: The guide brings Ezekiel “through the entry, which was at the side of the gate, into the holy rooms for the priests.” Arminian readers see the vision returning to the temple’s arrangements after the land rules.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the guide leading the prophet to the priests’ rooms. Readers in this tradition note that the place on the west side prepares for the explanation of the priests’ kitchens that follows.

verses.text: He said to me, “This is the place where the priests shall boil the trespass offering and the sin offering, and where they shall bake the meal offering, that they not bring them out into the outer court, to sanctify the people.”
verses.arminianNotes: “This is the place where the priests shall boil the trespass offering and the sin offering, and where they shall bake the meal offering.” Arminian readers see the priests’ portions prepared within the holy area, as their share in 44:29.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see holy food kept within holy space, “that they not bring them out into the outer court, to sanctify the people.” Readers in this tradition connect this with 44:19 on keeping holy things apart from the people.

verses.text: Then he brought me out into the outer court and caused me to pass by the four corners of the court; and behold, in every corner of the court there was a court.
verses.arminianNotes: The guide brings Ezekiel “out into the outer court” and shows him a smaller court in each of its four corners. Arminian readers see the vision turning to provision for the people’s worship in the outer court.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the outer court arranged for the people. Readers in this tradition note that the vision attends not only to the holiest places but also to the practical needs of ordinary worshipers.

verses.text: In the four corners of the court there were courts enclosed, forty cubits long and thirty wide. These four in the corners were the same size.
verses.arminianNotes: “In the four corners of the court there were courts enclosed, forty cubits long and thirty wide.” Arminian readers see measured, orderly spaces, consistent with the careful architecture throughout the vision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the precise measurements typical of the temple vision. Readers in this tradition do not press such details, but they see in them the order and care with which God’s house is arranged.

verses.text: There was a wall around in them, around the four, and boiling places were made under the walls all around.
verses.arminianNotes: “There was a wall around in them, around the four, and boiling places were made under the walls all around.” Arminian readers see cooking hearths built along the walls of the corner courts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see practical provision for preparing sacrificial meals. Readers in this tradition note that worship in the vision includes shared meals, a feature also found in the Torah’s peace offerings.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “These are the boiling houses, where the ministers of the house shall boil the sacrifice of the people.”
verses.arminianNotes: The guide explains, “These are the boiling houses, where the ministers of the house shall boil the sacrifice of the people.” Arminian readers see the people’s offerings prepared so that worshipers could share in the meal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Levites serving the people by preparing their sacrifices. Readers in this tradition note the distinction between these kitchens and the priests’ kitchens of 46:20, which keeps holy portions apart.
